common_name: Martha Washington Asparagus (Historic USDA Rust-Resistant Heirloom)

planting.note: Set dormant one-year crowns into trenches 6-8 inches deep as soon as soil is workable in spring, then gradually backfill as spears emerge.

directions: Martha Washington is a companion strain to the better-known Mary Washington, both bred in the early 1900s through USDA-led work with Massachusetts growers to overcome asparagus rust that had devastated eastern plantings. Like other old open-pollinated Washington strains it is dioecious, so female plants set seed and can self-sow into a weedy stand if spent berries are not removed each fall. Spears are thick and well-flavored but yields lag well behind modern all-male hybrids such as Jersey Knight or Millennium, since female plants divert energy into seed rather than spear production. Top-dress beds with compost each fall and let plants establish for a full year before taking any harvest, as with any asparagus crown.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Asparagus in the Home Garden
University of Illinois Extension — Watch Your Garden Grow: Asparagus
North Dakota State University Extension — Millennium Is the New Leader in Asparagus

common_name: Cherry Red Rhubarb (Sweet South Australian Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant dormant crown divisions in fall or very early spring into deep, rich, well-drained soil; Cherry Red needs a sustained period of winter chill below about 40F to break dormancy and crop well the following season.

directions: Cherry Red is a long-grown South Australian cultivar, cultivated commercially in the Adelaide Hills for decades, prized for stalks that are red through and through and notably sweeter and less tart than many older rhubarb strains. It forms a vigorous clump with thick, juicy stalks that color up fully even without heavy winter chilling by regional standards, though reliable cropping still depends on a real cold dormant period each year. Like all rhubarb it is not well suited to hot, mild-winter regions such as the Gulf Coast, where insufficient chill leads to thin, weak stalks and poor vigor; gardeners there are usually better served treating it as a short-lived annual grown from purchased crowns, if at all. Harvest by pulling stalks from the outside of the clump once established, leaving at least a third of the foliage intact to sustain the crown.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension — Rhubarb, Rheum rhabarbarum

common_name: Bianco Avorio Cardoon (Italian Spineless Ivory-White Cardoon)

planting.note: Start indoors six to eight weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger has passed into deep, fertile soil; Bianco Avorio's leaves are spineless and easy to handle compared with traditional spiny cardoons.

directions: Bianco Avorio, also sold as Ivory White cardoon, is an Italian heirloom selected for thick, meaty, ivory-pale leaf ribs and finely cut, nearly spineless silvery foliage that makes it almost as easy to handle as a thistle-free vegetable. The tall, architectural clump is ornamental in its own right even where it is not harvested, with deeply lobed gray-green leaves on stout stalks. About two weeks before harvest, blanch the bundled stalks by wrapping them in cardboard, newspaper, or straw to exclude light and mellow their flavor and texture, then cut the stalks at the base once pale and tender. In hot, humid, mild-winter climates like the Gulf Coast, cardoon is best grown as a cool-season annual started in fall or very early spring, since summer heat makes stalks tough and bitter and plants rarely overwinter as true perennials outside Mediterranean-type climates.
